title: Prognostic Performance of Inflammatory and Nutritional Indices for 30-Day Mortality According to Leukocytosis Status in Older Adults with Acute Abdomen: A Retrospective Cohort Study
content: Background and Objectives: In older adults with acute abdomen, classic examination and laboratory findings such as leukocytosis may be subtle or absent, yet mortality is higher than in younger patients. Inflammatory and nutritional indices derived from routine blood tests have been associated with mortality in several patient populations, but they do not appear to have been compared directly in older patients with acute abdomen. We compared four such indices to predict 30-day mortality in older patients hospitalized with acute abdomen diagnoses and examined whether their performance differed by leukocytosis status. Materials and Methods: This single-center retrospective cohort study included 1099 patients aged ≥65 years hospitalized with acute abdomen diagnoses between 2020 and 2026. We assessed the discrimination of the blood urea nitrogen-to-albumin ratio (BAR), C-reactive protein-to-albumin ratio (CAR), prognostic nutritional index (PNI) and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) with ROC analysis. Independent associations were examined with logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, diagnosis group and Charlson Comorbidity Index. Performance was compared according to leukocytosis status (white blood cell count >10 × 10³/µL), with Bonferroni correction. Results: Thirty-day mortality was 8.3% (n = 91). BAR had the highest discrimination (area under the curve [AUC] 0.82; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.78–0.87). AUCs for PNI, CAR and NLR were 0.71, 0.70 and 0.61, respectively. All four indices remained independently associated with mortality, with the strongest association for BAR (odds ratio [OR] per 1 standard deviation 2.86; 95% CI 2.23–3.67). BAR performed similarly regardless of leukocytosis status (AUC 0.83 and 0.82). PNI and CAR had numerically higher AUCs without leukocytosis, but neither difference reached the Bonferroni-corrected threshold. Conclusions: Among older patients hospitalized with acute abdomen diagnoses, BAR was the best discriminator of 30-day mortality, and its performance was similar regardless of leukocytosis status. The higher AUCs of PNI and CAR without leukocytosis are exploratory and require validation in external cohorts.
